1:
Which Herod this is has to be settled first, and Remigius states the difficulty plainly: we read long before that Herod was dead, and that on his death the Lord returned out of Egypt. The answer is that there were two. Archelaus succeeded the first and after ten years was sent into exile in Gaul, whereupon the kingdom was divided into tetrarchies among the sons; the Herod who beheaded John is the son of the greater Herod under whom the Lord was born, and the evangelist's own word tetrarch confirms it. Barnes and Clarke both note that the title properly means a ruler over a fourth part but is taken more generally by the Jewish writers, and Clarke observes that the estates were in fact divided into three. Ellicott fills in the rest: son of Herod the Great by Malthace, ruler of Galilee and Peræa, first married to a daughter of the Arabian king Aretas; Herodias, wife of his half-brother Philip, was daughter of the Aristobulus whom Herod had put to death and so niece to both her husbands. Prompted partly by passion and partly by ambition she left Philip for Antipas, in a marriage at once adulterous and by the Mosaic law doubly incestuous, which shocked the conscience of all the stricter Jews and drew Antipas into war with the father of the wife he had dismissed.

Why the news reached him so late is asked by nearly everyone. Chrysostom takes it for pride and carelessness, since those in authority, fenced about with much pomp, learn such things slowly because they do not much regard them. Barnes suggests absence on some expedition and adds that a man of such dissoluteness of morals paid little attention to the affairs of his people, and may have heard before without thinking it a matter worthy of regard. Ellicott thinks a tetrarch residing at Tiberias among courtiers might well be slow to hear of the Prophet of Nazareth, and guesses at the first informants, the nobleman of Capernaum, or Manaen the foster-brother, or Chuza the steward. Henry turns the delay into a rule: it is the unhappiness of the great ones of the world that they are most out of the way of hearing the best things, and God will honour those who are despised for his sake, the gospel like the sea getting in one place what it loses in another.

The verdict Herod reaches is where the commentators concentrate, because it contradicts his own creed. Lightfoot argues from the leaven of Herod being rendered elsewhere the leaven of the Sadducees that he held their doctrine, so that the words about John risen seem extorted from a conscience pricked with the sting of horror and guilt, forgetting his Sadduceeism and acknowledging the resurrection whether he will or no; and he adds that even those who confessed a resurrection did not dream of one so soon after death. Wesley says it in a line, that Sadduceeism staggers when conscience awakes. Clarke sees conscience performing the office of ten thousand accusers while offering no relief from God and pointing out no salvation from sin. Ellicott presses that this was neither a spectre from the unseen world nor the passing of John's soul into another body but John himself, and Jerome had already refused the doctrine of transmigration here, since the Lord was thirty years old when John was beheaded. Calvin alone declines to make the conjecture Herod's own, inferring from the other account that it was a report current among the people, to which their hatred of the tyrant and detestation of the murder had given rise.
3:
Where John was held is known from outside the Gospel. Ellicott and Robertson both cite Josephus for Machærus in Peræa as the scene of the imprisonment and the death, and Robertson adds what has been made of the site: an impregnable fortress on a high ridge where Herod the Great had built an extensive and beautiful palace, its windows commanding a wide prospect that took in the Dead Sea, the course of the Jordan and Jerusalem, with remains of two dungeons still there, one of them deep and its sides scarcely broken in, small holes visible in the masonry where staples of wood and iron had once been fixed. Matthew had recorded the bare fact of the imprisonment earlier without naming the place.

Who Herodias was is set out with care, since the charge depends on it. Barnes makes her a granddaughter of Herod the Great, first married to Herod Philip and mother by him of the Salome who probably danced, and follows Josephus for the occasion: Antipas stopped at his brother's house on a journey to Rome, fell in love with his wife, agreed to put away his own wife the daughter of Aretas, and Herodias agreed to leave her husband and live with him. Robertson corrects the identification of that first husband, who was Herod Philip of Rome and not Philip the Tetrarch, notes that he was still living, and calls the whole business a nasty mess equal to any of our modern divorces. Clarke names her parents as Aristobulus and Bernice and adds the sequel: when Aretas understood that his daughter was to be put away he prepared war, the two armies met, Herod's was cut to pieces by the Arabians, and Josephus says this was supposed to be a judgment of God on him for the murder of the Baptist. Barnes separates the two crimes, adultery because she was another man's wife and incest because marriage with so near a relation was expressly forbidden.

Why John was seized is the one point where the Gospel and the historian diverge, and Calvin states it squarely. The evangelists relate that John was seized because he had openly condemned the carrying off of Herodias and the incestuous marriage; Josephus assigns a different reason, that Herod, dreading a change of affairs on his own account, regarded John with suspicion. Calvin allows that this may have been the pretext on which the tyrant excused his crime, or a report in circulation, since various motives are frequently assigned for unjust violence and cruelty, but holds that the evangelists point out the true state of the fact; and he corrects the historian again for supposing Herodias was carried off from Herod king of Chalcis rather than from Philip, the crime being still recent when the evangelists wrote and committed before the eyes of all. Ellicott reports the historian's account in its more general form, that Antipas feared lest the preaching of the Baptist, working on the excitable peasantry of Galilee, should end in a popular outbreak. Origen draws a longer consequence from the killing: as the law and the prophets were until John, so the authority of those who ruled the people, which included the power to put to death, lasted until John, and when the last of the prophets was unlawfully killed that power was taken away, since otherwise Herod and the council would have sufficed and Pilate need never have condemned Jesus.
4:
What John actually said is brief, and every witness weighs it. Gill has him go to Herod and reprove him to his face, and for all the evils he had done besides, showing zeal for holiness and hatred of sin and courage in reproving so great a man freely, and making it manifest that he came in the spirit of Elijah. Lightfoot supplies the law behind the words: there are thirty-six cuttings off in the law, that is, sinners who deserve cutting off, and among them he that lies with his brother's wife; and he notes that Philip was then alive and lived on to the twentieth year of Tiberius. Wesley goes further than the verse does, holding it unlawful for either brother to have her, since her father Aristobulus was their own brother, and adds that John's words were rough like his raiment and that he would not break the force of truth by using soft words even to a king. Robertson reads the imperfect tense as meaning John said it repeatedly, a blunt and brave thing that cost him his head, though it is better to have a head like John's and lose it than to have an ordinary head and keep it.

Clarke turns the rebuke into a standing charge against court religion. Here is an instance of zeal, fidelity and courage highly worthy of imitation; plainness, mildness and modesty are the qualifications necessary when we reprove the great; and the best service a subject can render his prince is to lay before him, in the plainest but most respectful manner, what the law of God requires of him and what it forbids. From which he draws the sting: how unutterable must the punishment be of those who are chaplains to princes and great men, and who either flatter them in their vices or wink at their sins.

Why the sentence was not carried out at once is answered by the fear it ran up against. Gill has Herodias incensed and enraged, ready to kill John herself and hindered only by Herod, while Herod for his part was held back by the terror of his own conscience and by the respect he bore a good man. Ellicott follows Mark, whose narrative is fullest here: Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just man and holy, and was much perplexed, which Ellicott takes for the true reading, and heard him gladly; there was still a struggle of conscience against passion in the weak and wicked tetrarch, as there had been in Ahab with Elijah, whereas in Herodias, as in Jezebel, there was no halting between two opinions. Calvin reconciles the two accounts in sequence: at first Herod was unwilling and restrained by religious scruple, then shook off that fear of God under the incessant urging of Herodias, and then was withheld by a new restraint, the dread of a popular commotion; and he reads the phrase about her seeking an opportunity as meaning she worked by indirect wiles upon her husband's mind rather than openly. Clarke will not call the restraint a virtue: miserable prince, who fears more to offend his people than to sin against his God by shedding innocent blood, for when a man resists sin only by the help of human motives he cannot long defend himself.
6:
That a birthday is being kept is itself remarked on, and not kindly. Jerome notes that we find no others keeping their birthday besides Herod and Pharaoh, so that they who were alike in their wickedness might be alike in their festivities. Gill observes that the birthdays of princes, both of their coming into the world and of their accession, were kept by Egyptians, Persians and Romans but not by the Jews, who reckon these among the feasts of idolaters, and Lightfoot confirms it from the schools, which count the keeping of birthdays a part of idolatrous worship and list it with the Kalends and the Saturnalia. Clarke allows either sense of the word, the day of birth or the day of accession. Ellicott sees no reason to refuse the simple natural sense and adds that such feasts were common in imperial life at Rome, where Herod's own had become proverbial enough for a satirist to describe the banquet; Robertson confirms the usage from the papyri. Calvin is the one who pauses over the custom itself. There is nothing wrong in preparing an expensive banquet, and the ancient practice of marking the day each year cannot in itself be disapproved, since its return reminds us to thank God who brought us into the world, to recollect how uselessly the granted time has passed, and to commit the remainder to the same protection. But nothing is so pure that the world will not taint it with its own vices, and such is the tendency of the human mind to licentiousness that when the reins are loosened it quickly goes astray.

What kind of dance this was divides the witnesses sharply. Barnes calls it a violation of all the rules of modesty and propriety, since the governing principle of eastern nations is to keep women from public view, confined to their own part of the house and veiled so closely in public that the face cannot be seen; no modest woman would have appeared so before the court, and he thinks the dance was the lascivious and wanton one known in Greece as the Ionic. Ellicott agrees and sharpens it: dances in filmy garments that but half concealed the form were common enough at Eastern and Roman banquets, but the dancers were women who made it their calling, like the nautch-girls of India, and it was a new thing at which every decent Jew would shudder for the daughter of a kingly house to expose herself to the gaze of banqueters who included the chief captains of the legions. Robertson calls it a shameful exhibition of lewd dancing, prearranged, in which Salome stooped to the level of a common hired dancer, and both he and Clarke reach for the old English version that renders the verb with sovereign contempt, she leped in the myddle. Lightfoot alone reads it otherwise, as done not so much out of lightness as according to the custom of the nation, to express joy and celebrate the day, since the Jews expressed cheerfulness in their public rejoicings by leaping and dancing, and the chief part of the mirth at Tabernacles consisted in such dancing by the chief men and the aged and the most religious, the more vehemently the more commendably.

Where the blame falls is a separate question. Ellicott puts it on the mother, who knew the tetrarch's weak point as Madame du Barry knew that of Louis XV and sought to bend him to her will even at the cost of her daughter's modesty. Remigius divides it between them: mothers poor as well as rich bring their daughters up so chastely that they are scarce seen by strangers, but this unchaste woman taught hers not chastity but dancing, and Herod is no less to be blamed, who forgot that his was a royal palace while she made it a theatre.
7:
The oath is treated as a crime in its own right. Barnes calls it foolish and wicked, since to please a wanton girl the monarch called the eternal God to witness his willingness to give away half his kingdom and to shed the holiest blood it contained; such an oath was not lawful to make, and it should have been broken. Isidore states the principle behind that judgement in three clauses: in evil promises break faith, for that promise is impious which must be kept by crime, and that oath is not to be observed by which we have unwittingly pledged ourselves to evil. Lightfoot supplies the Talmudic name for it, a rash oath, and notices a grim fitness if the form used was the usual one, by his head, since the request then answered the promise exactly. Clarke recalls that the kings of Persia were accustomed to reject no petition preferred to them during the entertainment. Ellicott guesses at what Herod thought he was risking: the scandalous chronicles of the time were not without stories of extravagant rewards paid to mimes and dancers, and he may have fancied that here too he was reproducing the magnificence of the imperial court, with a jewel, a bracelet, a palace or a city in his mind as what she would be likely to ask.

How far the girl was in the plot turns on one word, and two witnesses correct the English. Ellicott renders it prompted or instigated rather than instructed beforehand, and denies that it implies she knew what to ask before she danced, since the other account says plainly that she went out from the banquet-hall to ask her mother what use she should make of the promise; he draws a further inference from the mother's absence, that the supper was for men only, and that it was among them, flushed with wine, that the daughter had appeared. Barnes says the same, not before she danced but afterwards, and grants that the only appearance of anything right in the whole transaction was her honouring her mother by consulting her, though she did it to accomplish the purposes of wickedness more effectually. Gill has her go out at once and come back straightway with haste, to take the king at his word while he was still in the mood, urged on by a mother eager to satisfy her revenge. Wesley reads the abruptness of the demand the same way: she says give me here, fearing that if he had time to consider he would not do it.

The dish and the custom behind it get more attention than one might expect. Clarke complains of the English word, which formerly meant a large dish or bowl or drinking cup and now conveys nothing, preferring the Saxon dish or the older platter, and Robertson asks the same question more bluntly. Barnes explains why a head should be produced at all: princes then required the heads of the executed to be brought to them, both to gratify their resentment by feasting their eyes on the proof that an enemy was dead and to ascertain that the sentence had actually been carried out. He adds a parallel from Roman history, Agrippina sending an officer to kill the woman who had been her rival for the imperial dignity, and then examining the head with her own hands until she perceived the feature by which she knew her. Clarke supplies the indignation the others leave out, at a mother who would give such instructions to a child, a daughter apt enough to receive them, and such a present for a young lady as the bloody head of the forerunner of Jesus.
9:
The king's sorrow is taken at face value by most and refused by one. Gill lists what it might have rested on: a lingering respect for John despite the freedom of his reproofs, a conscience telling him the act was evil and would leave a brand of perpetual infamy, fear of a people much attached to the prisoner, and even a Roman scruple, since it was reckoned an ill omen to take away life on the day one received one's own, so that executions were carefully avoided on such days. Barnes allows the first three and adds that a great and manifest crime was being proposed deliberately, to gratify the malice of a wicked woman and pay for a few moments' entertainment, so that conscience checked him in feeble and dying accents. Ellicott calls it the last struggle of conscience, in which his old reverence for the prophet and the joy that had once accompanied better strivings must have risen before him. Jerome alone will not have it: it is the manner of Scripture to speak of events as they were commonly viewed at the time, and Herod is said to be sorry because the guests believed him so, this dissembler of his own inclinations displaying sorrow in his face when he had joy in his mind.

What the oath was worth is the second question, and here nobody defends him. Barnes states the principle exactly: Herod felt bound, but he was not, for the oath should never have been taken, and being taken could not bind, since a prior obligation not to commit murder cannot be dissolved by any act of ours. Clarke notices that the word stands in the plural, so that he had probably sworn again and again, one sin begetting many, and thinks the guests would have counted it a breach of honour had he drawn back. Robertson judges the swearing more like profane swearing than the deliberate utterance of a solemn oath, from a man probably maudlin with wine and befuddled by the presence of his guests. Ellicott finds the real motive not in the oath at all, which if taken in secret he might have got over, but in his shrinking from the taunt or whispered jest or contemptuous gesture of the assembled guests, a false regard for what a narrow circle will say of us serving here, as so often, as an incentive to guilt instead of a restraint. Jerome presses the same point harder by a question: had she asked the death of her mother or her father, would he have granted it? And he reads the mention of the guests as deliberate, that Herod would have them all sharers in his crime. Wesley compresses the whole into one line, that he murdered an innocent man from mere tenderness of conscience.

On the execution itself Gill identifies the officer sent, the speculator of the Latin writers, whose particular business was beheading. Lightfoot raises a difficulty of distance: if John lay at Machærus on the utmost bounds of Peræa while the court was at Tiberias, the journey could scarcely be done in two days, so that the head cannot have been presented to the girl until some days after the feast. Ellicott stands back and gives the verdict the Gospel implies, that of one who had preached in the wilderness only a few short months it must be said, as of the kings and conquerors of the world, that so passed from the earth one of the greatest of her sons.
11:
Where the head was brought from is a small point on which two witnesses part. Gill infers from its arrival while the company were still at table that the prison must have been very near, and thinks it not improbable that the entertainment was held in the castle of Machærus itself; Lightfoot, reckoning the court at Tiberias, had made the same nearness impossible. Raban reports both halves of the tradition, that Josephus has John sent bound to that castle and beheaded there, while ecclesiastical history has him buried at Sebastia in Palestine, the town formerly called Samaria.

What the mother did with it draws the sharpest language in the chapter. Robertson describes Herodias witnessing with fiendish delight the triumph of an implacable hatred, and dismisses the legends that picture Salome as herself in love with John as resting on no proof. Clarke generalises from her to a class, that there is no person so revengeful as a lascivious woman when reproved and blamed, and warns that a preacher of the gospel has most to fear from that quarter, since the first of the profession lost his life for the sake of truth and chastity; he also passes on Jerome's report that she drew out the tongue and thrust it through with her bodkin. Ellicott prefers to follow the accomplices into their after-history. When her brother obtained the title of king through the favour of Caligula, Herodias, consistent in her ambition, stirred up her husband to seek the same honour and went with him to Rome; complaints from the oppressed Galileans followed them, he was deposed from his tetrarchy and banished to Lugdunum in Gaul, and she went with him, faithful to his fallen fortunes in spite of her brother's overtures, and there they died. Of the daughter, Ellicott notes that a legend makes her death retributive, a fall upon ice that severed her head from her body, while Josephus records only her two marriages.

The disciples of John do two things, and both are weighed. Gill supposes they applied to Herod for the body as Joseph of Arimathea afterwards applied to Pilate, and were allowed to take it. Barnes gives three reasons why they then went to Jesus: the event was important and bound up with his work, they were in affliction and came for consolation, which he commends as an example to follow, and they feared that one engaged in the same cause stood in the same danger. Robertson adds that it was a shock to the Master, who alone knew how great John really was, and that the fate of the forerunner was a prophecy of what lay before him. Ellicott counts the transfer of allegiance as permanent, believing the two whom John had sent from prison were among them, and dates from here the end of the Baptist's followers as a distinct community in Judæa, though Apollos and the disciples at Ephesus show that a separate existence persisted in more distant regions. Gregory stands back from the narrative to wonder at it: that one filled with the spirit of prophecy in his mother's womb should be beheaded because of the dancing of a girl, and that a man of such severe life should die for the sport of shameful men. God oppresses his people in the least things, he answers, because he sees how he may reward them in the highest; and though John was not sought out to suffer for the confession of Christ but for the truth of righteousness, because Christ is truth he went to death for Christ in going for truth.
13:
Whether the withdrawal was flight is the question the chapter turns on here, and the answers are not the same. Gill takes the occasion simply: Jesus heard of John's death and cruel usage, and that his own fame had reached the court. Henry sharpens it, that he withdrew on hearing not of the death but of the thoughts Herod had formed about him, and departed further off to get out of Herod's jurisdiction; in times of peril, when God opens a door of escape, it is lawful to flee for our own preservation unless we have some special call to expose ourselves, and since his hour was not yet come he would not thrust himself upon suffering. Henry adds the detail that matters most to him: he could have secured himself by divine power, but because his life was intended for an example he did it by human prudence. Clarke agrees it was not fear, and reads it as teaching his messengers to yield to the storm rather than expose themselves where the case is hopeless. Jerome offers three readings in succession and refuses the first outright: not through fear of death, as some suppose, but in mercy to his enemies, that they might not add murder to murder, putting off his death until the day of the passion; or to leave us an example against the rashness that makes men surrender themselves voluntarily, since not all persevere under torture with the constancy with which they offered themselves to it; or to prove the faith of believers, who followed on foot rather than riding, with the toil of their own legs. And the evangelist's own word, he adds, is not fled but withdrew, showing that he shunned rather than feared persecution. Chrysostom looks past the danger altogether: the withdrawal prolonged the economy of his humanity, the time not being yet come for openly manifesting his deity, and though he knew of himself what had been done he did not move until it was told him, that the verity of the incarnation might be confirmed by his actions and not by his appearance only.

Two witnesses decline to make the death of John the whole reason. Calvin notes that one Gospel gives no reason while two others make the journey a rest for the disciples after their return from their embassy, and finds no contradiction, since both may hold at once; he adds that minds still feeble might well have been terrified by the melancholy end of so eminent a prophet. Wesley lists three motives together, to avoid Herod, to escape the pressing multitude, and to talk with disciples newly returned. Ellicott adds the personal one the others leave unsaid, the strong emotion which the death of a man Jesus had known and loved could not fail to cause, together with the wish not to become the centre of a popular excitement so strong that men afterwards read the troubles of Antipas as a judgment for the murder; and he notes that the Passover was coming on, thronging the roads of Galilee with pilgrims.

Where he went is Lightfoot's subject, and he corrects the maps. The crossing was from Capernaum to the desert of Bethsaida, which another Gospel describes as going over the sea, properly understood as passing from Galilee into Peræa; the chorographical maps place Bethsaida in Galilee on the same coast as Capernaum, an opinion Lightfoot once shared, until Josephus taught him that it lay in upper Gaulanitis on the eastern shore. The objection that the multitude could not then have followed on foot he answers by the route: they crossed at the bridge of Jordan in Chammath, a mile or less from Tiberias and some three miles from Capernaum. Barnes describes the country plainly, a large tract east of the sea, rough and uncultivated and chiefly used for pasturing flocks.
14:
The movement of the verse is toward the crowd rather than away from it, and Ellicott marks the turn. The words imply that from the height to which he had withdrawn our Lord saw the crowds drawing near, and then, instead of retiring further, went forward to meet them, moved by the pity which the sight of an eager and suffering multitude never failed to rouse in him. Gill weighs where exactly he came out from, the mountain where he sat with his disciples, or the desert where he had retired, or the ship, which he thinks likeliest since the company had reached the place before the landing.

The word for his compassion is one the commentators will not pass over. Clarke says it should generally be rendered tender compassion, notes that as a verb it seems not to have been used by any but ecclesiastical writers, and explains that it always intimates that motion of the bowels, accompanied with extreme tenderness and concern, which is felt at the sight of another's misery. Robertson says the same more briefly, that the verb carries the oriental idea of the bowels as the seat of compassion, and glosses the sick as those without strength.

What it was that moved him is drawn from the parallel account, where the ground of the compassion is that they were as sheep having no shepherd. Barnes unfolds the figure at length: a shepherd feeds his flock, defends it from wolves and wild beasts, cares for the young and the feeble, and leads it by green pastures and still waters; to say the people were without one is to say they had no teachers and guides who cared for them or took pains to instruct them, since the scribes and Pharisees were proud and cared little for the common people, and when they did teach them led them astray. That, he concludes, is why they came in such multitudes to one who preached the gospel to the poor and was himself the good Shepherd. Calvin reads it the same way and adds a qualification: Christ saw famishing souls whom zeal had carried from their homes, and the scarcity of teaching indicated a wretched state of disorder; not that in his divine nature he looked on them all as sheep, but that as man he judged according to the present aspect of the case. Calvin also counts their coming as no small manifestation of piety, since they left their own homes and flocked to the Prophet of God though he had purposely concealed himself from them.

What the healing shows is left to Chrysostom, who measures it against the zeal that earned it. Great as was the affection of those who had left their cities and sought him carefully, the things done for them surpassed the reward of any zeal; and it is great compassion, he adds, to heal all and not to require faith. Calvin notices what the healing cost: Christ was fatigued and almost worn out by uninterrupted toil and had sought some relaxation on his own account as well as for his disciples, yet when urgent duty called him to further labour he willingly set that private consideration aside.
15:
Which evening is meant has to be fixed before anything else, because the chapter uses the word twice. Gill notes with Grotius that the Jews had two, the first beginning when the sun declined at noon and the second at sunset, and argues that this is the earlier one, since a second evening comes on later in the story and the disciples' proposal that the people go and buy food would make no sense after dark. Robertson agrees and puts the hour at about three, and Barnes glosses the phrase about the time being past as meaning that the day was wearing away, or that the usual hour of refreshment had gone by.

The desert is not incidental either. Chrysostom makes the place part of the proof: the Lord led them out there so that the miracle might be clear of all suspicion and nobody suppose that anything had been supplied from a neighbouring town, and he recalls what was proverbial among the Jews for the impossible, whether God could spread a table in the wilderness. Robertson keeps the geography modest, a lonely and comparatively uninhabited stretch rather than a desolate one, with villages near enough to buy in but too far to reach in time. Chrysostom reads the waiting as evidence on both sides. That the crowds endured hunger until evening proves their faith; that none of them approached with a request he explains by their awe and by a zeal in which they did not feel their hunger; and that the Lord, purposing to feed them, waited to be asked is his settled rule, since he does not step forward first to work miracles but acts when he is called upon.

What the disciples actually proposed is read generously by some and as a failure by others. Clarke takes their concern for the people's bodies as a credit to them, holding that no man is worthy to be called a minister of Christ who does not promote both the temporal and the spiritual welfare of those he serves to the uttermost of his power; and he infers from the crowd's willingness to leave home and go without food that the preaching must have been accompanied with uncommon power. Chrysostom is harder: even the disciples do not come and say, give them to eat, for they were as yet in an imperfect condition, and could only say that the place was desert. Calvin sees a purpose in the delay itself. Christ had put off the miracle until now so that his disciples might consider it more attentively and derive greater advantage from it, and so that the timing might teach them that though he does not prevent their wants, and does not always supply them at once, he never ceases to care for his people but has the help at hand at the very moment it is required.

Ellicott stops before the miracle to say why this narrative matters more than most. It is the only miracle recorded by all four evangelists; it is the fullest manifestation of the sovereignty of the Son of Man over the world of nature, an act of creative power that cannot be explained away, as some healings might be, as the effect of strong faith or excited imagination in those who received it; and the one rationalising account ever offered, that the example of the five loaves shamed the crowd into producing stores each man had selfishly concealed, he calls ludicrously inadequate. The narrative, he concludes, must be accepted or rejected as a whole. Augustine meanwhile settles the one point where the accounts appear to differ, the question put to Philip which only the fourth Gospel records: suppose that after the words reported here the Lord looked on the multitude and said what that Gospel relates, and no one need be perplexed when one evangelist relates what the rest have omitted.
16:
The command is read by everyone as deliberately impossible. Robertson points to the emphasis in the Greek, which sets the disciples over against their own proposal: they had said send away, and the answer puts the stress on give ye them to eat, in the urgent aorist of instant action. He calls it an astounding command, and takes its lesson to be that no situation appears desperate to Christ and no crisis unmanageable. Barnes fills in from the fourth Gospel what lay behind it, the question put to Philip in order to prove him, that is, to test his faith; Philip fell at once to reckoning, and judged that two hundred denarii would not buy enough, a sum Barnes works out at something near twenty-eight dollars and calls great in the eyes of twelve poor fishermen. It was that arithmetic, he insists, and not any unwillingness to provide, which had made the disciples ask that the crowd be sent away; and the answer requires of them, as of us, that we simply do what Christ commands, without doubting that he will give strength to accomplish it.

Clarke turns the same words into an address to ministers. He who seeks first the kingdom is sure of every temporal requisite, and when a man secures the first, God throws the other into the bargain; so that when the means by which men help their fellows have failed we are not to suppose the bounty of God exhausted. Should we ask how feeble servants are to feed so many hungry souls, his answer is to begin at the command, make the attempt, divide what you have, and the bread of God will be multiplied in your hands. Origen reads the exchange as a lesson in what the disciples had not yet grasped. They did not deny that they could give loaves, but thought five much too few; what they failed to consider was that when Jesus takes each loaf, which is the Word, he extends it as far as he wills and makes it suffice for all whom he desires to nourish.

Calvin draws the pastoral conclusion and then guards it. Until now Christ had given his whole attention to feeding souls; here he takes the care even of their bodies into his duties as a shepherd, confirming his own saying that to those who seek the kingdom of God all other things shall be added. But we have no right to expect that he will always follow this method of supplying the hungry, only that he will never let his own people want the necessaries of life and will stretch out his hand from heaven when he sees it needful. Those who wish to have Christ for their provider, Calvin adds, must first learn not to long for refined luxuries but to be satisfied with barley-bread.

The older readers hear the five loaves and two fishes as a figure. Hilary takes the loaves for the five books of the Law and the fishes for the preaching of the Prophets and of John, and explains the disciples' helplessness by the same scheme, that it was not yet given them to minister the heavenly bread, so that they were still confined to what they had; from these things, he says, the preaching of the Gospel grows to its more abundant strength. Raban makes the two fishes the Prophets and the Psalms, the whole of the older Scriptures being comprehended in the three, and finds the point in what was not done: being asked for food, Christ creates no new viands but takes what the disciples already had and gives thanks, just as when he came in the flesh he preached no other things than had been foretold, and only showed that the old writings were big with mysteries.
17:
The answer the disciples give is read as an excuse. Gill says plainly that they spoke to excuse themselves and to show the impossibility of feeding so large a number, and Robertson observes that they were quick with reasons for their inability, as we are still. Barnes fills in what the fourth Gospel adds about the provisions: the loaves were in the hands of a lad, most probably one who had food to sell among the multitude rather than an attendant carrying the apostles' own, and they were of barley, a cheap grain scarcely a third the value of wheat and much used by poor people; fish, he adds, would have been a considerable part of the diet of people living on the borders of a lake that abounded in it. Lightfoot declines to say what kind of fish these were, but notes that the Talmudists discourse much of salt fish, and that a tradition about blessing salted food before the morsel that accompanies it would be worth comparing with the form of blessing Christ used here, if only it could be shown that these were salted. Clarke turns the shortage into a lesson: when we are deeply conscious of our own necessities we are led to depend on Jesus with a firmer faith, and God often permits his servants to be brought low that they may have repeated opportunities of proving the kindness of their Master.

The reply is three words long and the commentators weigh each of them. Robertson marks the contrast between the helpless doubt of the disciples and the confident courage of Jesus, who takes up the very five loaves and two fishes they had named as their reason for doing nothing; they had simply overlooked his power in the emergency. Gill reads the command as a test, of their faith in him, their obedience to him and their liberality toward others, and draws from it the rule he wants remembered: the best way to have an increase of temporal supplies is to bring what we have and put it into Christ's hands, whereby good is done to others and returned to the giver with an overplus. Clarke says the same in his own key. No creature of God should be reckoned good or safe without the blessing of God in it, so that if you have but a handful of meal and a few herbs, bring them to Christ by prayer and faith and he will make them a sufficiency for the body and a sacrament to the soul; and let the minister of the gospel do likewise with his gifts and graces, knowing that his word can be of no use unless the blessing of Christ be in it.
19:
The arrangement of the crowd is treated as deliberate rather than incidental. Gill harmonises the accounts by having both orders given, Christ commanding the multitude to sit, which they would never have done otherwise, and the disciples enjoined to place them in ranks by hundreds and by fifties, so that their number might be the better taken and the food more orderly distributed. Barnes corrects the English, since the word is to recline as at a meal, the Jews never sitting as we do. Ellicott notices the calm and orderly precision of it and passes on the other evangelist's picture of the result, companies looking like so many beds of flowers in a well-ordered garden, a resemblance the bright colours of Eastern dress would have made more striking than it could be among ourselves. Robertson sets the scene in the afternoon sun on a grassy hillside sloping westward, with Jesus standing where all could see him break the thin Jewish cakes.

What the blessing was is the one point of dispute. Barnes takes the word in its common sense of giving thanks, and turns it into a pattern: to seek a blessing on food is to pray that it may nourish us, that we may be properly grateful to the Giver, and that we may remember the Creator while partaking of the bounties of his providence, and our Saviour always sought such a blessing, so what he did we should do. Clarke identifies the act as that of the father of a family among the Jews, whose business it was to take the bread and render thanks before any of the household tasted it, and he presses a point of translation: the word to be supplied is God rather than them, since it does not appear that Christ blessed the loaves but rather the God who had provided them, the Jewish custom being to bless not the food but the giver. He grants that others take the loaves to be meant, and that he blessed them in order to multiply them, and he prints the Hebrew form of grace before meat as a comparison. Calvin agrees that the word denotes thanksgiving and draws the sharper conclusion, that we cannot partake of food with holiness unless we express gratitude to the hand it comes from; unbelievers corrupt by the filth of their unbelief what is by nature pure, and are corrupted in turn by what they swallow. Of the lifted eyes he says that such an attitude is not at all times necessary in prayer, but that the Son of God did not choose to disregard outward forms fitted to aid human weakness, and that looking upward rouses us from sloth when our minds are too strongly fixed on the earth. Clarke reads the same gesture as teaching us to acknowledge God as the Supreme Good and fountain of all excellence.

Where the multiplication happened is a question two of the older readers cannot resist. Jerome observes that the Lord calls the apostles to the breaking so that the greatness of the miracle might be the more evident on their own testimony that they had nothing, and that in the breaking there is a sowing of food, for had the loaves stayed whole and not been divided into a manifold harvest they could never have fed so great a multitude. Hilary confesses he cannot tell: the five loaves are not multiplied into more, but fragments succeed to fragments, the substance growing either upon the tables or in the hands that took them up, he knows not which.
20:
That everyone was satisfied is where the witnesses locate the proof. Barnes calls it an undoubted miracle, since the quantity must have been greatly increased to supply so many, and argues that he who could increase it so far had the power of creation itself. Clarke presses the same point against two evasions: there was a manifest creation of substance, for the parts of the bread were not dilated to make them appear large, and there was no delusion in the eating, since they all ate and were all filled; here then is one miracle attested by at least five thousand persons. Robertson notes that the verb for being filled comes from the word for grass, and insists that the broken pieces gathered afterwards were not scraps from the ground but the pieces Jesus himself had broken and nobody had eaten. Lightfoot supplies a Talmudic definition of a proper meal, which is when they eat their fill, along with the saying that all eating where salt is not is not eating.

The baskets get more attention than the bread. Ellicott identifies the word as the small hand-basket that travellers used for their food, and quotes the Roman satirist who describes the Jews of Italy travelling with their basket and a wisp of hay for a pillow; Robertson adds that Wycliff called them coffins, and that a different and larger word is used at the later feeding of the four thousand. Barnes explains the custom by the conditions of travel, since a Jew could expect little hospitality among Gentiles or Samaritans, and the caravansaries were meant for lodging rather than food. Both he and Clarke pass on the conjecture that each of the apostles filled his own, and Clarke reports the further notion that the Jews carried baskets in memory of the Egyptian bondage. On why the fragments were gathered at all, Ellicott takes the express command that nothing be lost to mean that a display of creative power was not to supersede forethought, thrift and economy in the use of what it had given, and thinks the fragments were probably reserved for the poor, whom the disciples seem to have been in the habit of relieving. Barnes reaches it from the nature of food itself, which God creates and which therefore has a kind of sacredness. Calvin sees the leftovers as part of the design: more than twelve times what had been put into their hands remained, so that all might know the power of Christ had provided not only for immediate use but, if required, for future wants, and that a striking proof should survive the miracle to be contemplated at leisure once the crowd had been refreshed.

The count at the end is exact in one respect and vague in another. Gill notes that the word about is omitted in several versions, which say simply that there were so many, and calls it a large number to be fed with five loaves and two fishes. Ellicott observes that Matthew alone mentions the women and children, that all four evangelists use the word which emphasises that the five thousand were men, and suggests that since many had come from considerable distances the women and children were few, grouped by themselves and not counted, so that the round number stayed in men's minds without reference to them. Robertson insists that the phrase does not mean they were not fed. Origen finds the expression genuinely ambiguous, allowing either that no woman or child was present at all or that only the men were reckoned, as those of twenty years are in the Book of Numbers. Barnes guesses the whole company may have been ten thousand, and records the effect the fourth Gospel reports, that they were convinced by it he was the prophet who should come into the world.
22:
The force of the word is the first thing noticed, and the reason for it comes from another Gospel. Robertson renders it compelled or forced, and explains it by the crowd's excited purpose of taking Jesus and making him a national king, which would have been political revolution and would have defeated all his plans; the disciples, he thinks, had been swept off their feet by the mood of the mob, still sharing the Pharisaic hope, so that with them out of the way he could handle the crowd more easily. Gill presses it further: the people, convinced by the miracle that he was the Messiah, were determined whether he would or not to set him up as a temporal deliverer, and the disciples had imbibed the same notion and would readily have joined them, so that it was with much difficulty they were brought off it and Christ had to use his authority. Lightfoot says briefly that they as yet dreamed too much of an earthly kingdom. Barnes dissents on the word itself, holding that it means here to command rather than to compel, since there was no need of compulsion.

Why the disciples were unwilling is answered differently by those who grant it. Clarke offers two possibilities, that they feared returning into Herod's jurisdiction or that they would not embark without their Lord, and notes besides that Christ must have given the multitudes counsel after their departure which he did not wish them to hear. Jerome takes it as love rather than fear, that they left unwillingly, not desiring to be parted from their teacher even for a moment, and adds that they were right to be slow, lest they suffer shipwreck while he was not with them. Henry says they were loth to go to sea without him and puts the prayer of Moses into their mouths, that if his presence went not with them they should not be carried up hence; he observes too that until the disciples were gone the people would not stir, and that Christ sent the crowd away with a blessing. Calvin makes their reluctance the point of the whole verse: they would never of their own accord have left him, and it had every appearance of absurdity that he should be left alone with night coming on, so that their yielding against their own opinion is the more commendable, since we do not truly obey God unless we follow whatever he commands though our feelings are opposed, there being always the best reason for what he does even when he conceals it for a time.

The withdrawal to the mountain is read by two witnesses as a spiritual necessity rather than a retreat. Barnes observes that at the very moment when human honours were almost forced upon him he retired for private prayer, and calls it an example for everyone pressed with honours and applause, nothing keeping the mind humble like shutting out the world in some lonely place. Ellicott presses further: in this unwonted stir of popular excitement, not against him but in his favour, this nearness to a path of earthly greatness instead of the one that led on to the cross, he saw something like a renewal of the temptation in the wilderness, and desired to pass through the conflict alone, as afterwards in Gethsemane, with no human eye to witness either the temptation or the victory. Chrysostom finds a plainer purpose in the separation, that those who had beheld the feeding should be away when the next sign was wrought, since it could never afterwards be urged that he had worked it fantastically in their presence; and he draws a rule from it, that when the Lord works a great miracle he sends the multitudes away, teaching us never to pursue their praise.
23:
Whether the crowd actually went is a detail Gill will not let pass. Christ ordered them away, but they did not generally disperse; a large body stayed on the spot all night expecting his return, and when that hope failed took shipping and came to Capernaum. Lightfoot marks the word for evening as bearing a different sense here from the one it bore earlier in the chapter: there it denoted the lateness of the day, here the lateness of the night, and among the Talmudists the same term covers the night itself, as their rule for reciting the phylacteries in the evening shows, which runs on to midnight or even to the rising of the pillar of the morning.

Why he prayed at all, having just done what he did, is the question Calvin faces. It is probable, he says, that the Son of God, fully aware of the tempest that was coming, did not neglect the safety of his disciples in his prayers, and we naturally wonder that he did not rather prevent the danger than employ himself in praying. The answer is in the office: discharging every part of his work as Mediator, he showed himself both God and man and gave proofs of each nature as occasion offered, so that though he had all things at his disposal he showed himself man by praying, and not hypocritically but with sincere human affection towards us, his divine majesty being for a time concealed and displayed afterwards at the proper moment. Clarke answers from the other end, the danger of success: he whom God has employed in a work of mercy has need to return by prayer as speedily as he can to his Maker, lest he be tempted to value himself on account of that in which he has no merit. Robertson makes it a matter of need rather than of pattern, since the masses were wild with enthusiasm and the disciples had wholly misunderstood him, so that if ever he wanted his Father's sympathy it was now, and the Father alone could offer help.

The place and the hour are read as instruction. Chrysostom calls the wilderness the mother of quiet, a calm and a harbour that delivers us from all turmoils, and takes the continual withdrawing into it as teaching us to seek in our prayers whatever quietness time and place can confer. Clarke turns the same observation into a list of what is wanted for praying well, retirement from the world, elevation of the heart to God, solitude, and the silence of the night, and adds that other society should be shut out when a soul comes to converse with God. Calvin makes the practical point that lies under it: we know how easily the slightest interruptions destroy the ardour of prayer, or at least make it languish and cool, and though Christ was in no danger of that fault he meant to warn us by his example to use every help for setting our minds free from the snares of the world.

What the solitude cost the disciples is Chrysostom's last observation, and he draws it out as a method. Before this they had been in the storm with him in the ship, though asleep, so that relief was ready to hand; now they are alone by themselves, and he leads them gently and by degrees to a greater endurance, departing and permitting the storm to arise in mid sea so that they might not so much as look for hope of preservation from any quarter. Hilary hears in the solitude a foreshadowing instead, that his being alone in the evening signifies his sorrow at the time of the passion, when the rest were scattered from him in fear.
24:
How far out they were is fixed from the fourth Gospel. Gill reports the versions, one saying many furlongs from land and another about twenty-five, and Barnes works the figure into miles, some four of them, noting that since the lake was nowhere more than ten miles broad they were literally in the midst of it. Ellicott makes the number nearly three-fourths of the way across and observes that it reads like a personal reminiscence, set down to guard against the explanations that would minimise what follows, such as that our Lord was seen walking on the shore or was swimming out to the boat. Of the boat's condition the witnesses agree and differ only in force: Ellicott renders the word literally as vexed or tormented, Clarke as grievously agitated, and notes one manuscript that reads instead plunged under the waves; Robertson uses the word that elsewhere describes a man tormented by demons, and pictures the craft bobbing up and down in the choppy sea.

The hour is given in a reckoning that needs explaining. Barnes and Clarke both set out the older Jewish division of the night into three watches, each of four hours, with the first, middle and morning watches all named in the Old Testament, and observe that a fourth is nowhere mentioned there, the four-watch division of three hours each having come in with the Romans, so that the watches were called evening, midnight, cock-crowing and morning. Ellicott dates the change from the conquest by Pompeius and fixes the hour between three and six, in the dimness of the early dawn. Lightfoot qualifies the whole account: the Jews acknowledge only three watches because they counted the fourth part of the night as morning rather than as night, so that there were in truth four watches but only three of deep night, which is why Gideon's middle watch was in fact the second of the four. Barnes and Clarke both draw the same inference from the timing, that Jesus had spent almost the whole night alone on the mountain in prayer.

On the walking itself nobody hedges. Clarke calls the suspension of the laws of gravitation a proper manifestation of unlimited power, done by Christ's own power and therefore a showing forth of his Godhead, and counts three miracles in the one: that at a distance he knew their distress, that he found them on the lake probably in the midst of darkness, and that he walked upon the water, as Job says of God that he treadeth upon the waves of the sea. Robertson reports the attempt to explain it away by supposing Jesus was merely walking along the beach and calls it an impossible theory unless the account is legendary. Ellicott states the alternatives without softening them, simple acceptance of the supernatural fact as another instance of his sovereignty or rejection of it as legend; taking the first, he sees in it something like an anticipation of that spiritual body which appeared again at the Transfiguration, became normal after the Resurrection and reached its completeness at the Ascension, and admits that one speculates almost involuntarily whether the ordinary laws of motion were broken, suspended, or counteracted by higher ones. Calvin looks rather at what the delay was for: the adverse wind rose about midnight and Christ did not appear until three hours before sunrise, so that their arms were not more fatigued by rowing than their faith was shaken by terror, and the long waiting was meant to fix their attention the more powerfully on the help he brought.
26:
What they could actually see is worked out before what they made of it. Gill supposes it was now morning and perhaps moonlit, and notes that there is always more light on water than on land, so that they could discern something like a man walking on the surface but not enough to tell who; and they had no thought of Christ or expectation of seeing him. Barnes sets the scene the same way, the form of a man in the dark night amidst tumultuous billows, and explains their conclusion from the beliefs of the time, since it was common among the ancients to hold that the spirits of men appeared to the living after death. Robertson strengthens the verb, which means not merely troubled but terrified, identifies the noun as spectre or ghost, and puts their outcry down to a little touch of sailor superstition. Clarke will not have it called superstition at all: that the spirits of the dead might and did appear was a doctrine held by the greatest and holiest of men that ever existed, and one which the cavillers and free-thinkers of different ages have never been able to disprove. Jerome turns the same fear into an argument against the heretics who denied that the Lord was born of a virgin and made him a phantasm, since the apostles here plainly feared they were seeing what those men said he was.

The answer comes at once, and the promptness is part of it. Gill stresses that he spoke the very moment they cried out, calling aloud as one truly affected toward them, since he had not come to frighten them but to save them. Clarke says nothing else in such circumstances could have given courage and comfort, and applies it to those grievously tossed with difficulties and temptations, who need a like manifestation of his power, for when he proclaims himself in the soul all sorrow and fear are at an end. Ellicott takes the exact agreement of three evangelists in reporting the words as proof of the impression they made; to hear the familiar tones amid the howling of the winds was enough to give confidence, and in after years the moment must have come back to them, and to the Church at large, with something of a symbolic character, so that Be of good cheer became the watchword of their lives.

Calvin examines what the reassurance actually does. Christ is not known as a Deliverer until he makes his appearance, and so he speaks and asks to be recognised, founding the confidence he urges on his presence alone; and he corrects their terror first, not because they could all at once lay aside fear and feel unmingled joy, but because the fear had to be allayed lest it destroy their confidence. The same voice, Calvin adds, is deadly to the reprobate and his presence appalling, while on believers the effect is widely different; and the reason we are disturbed by sudden and unfounded alarms is that our own ingratitude keeps us from using as shields the innumerable gifts of God, which if turned to account would give us all the support we need. Hilary reads the whole night as a figure of history, the four watches standing for the Law, the Prophets, the coming in the flesh and the return in glory, so that Christ at the end shall find his Church wearied and tossed by the spirit of Anti-Christ, and, troubled by long experience of deceit, afraid even at his own approach until he banishes the fear by saying who he is.
28:
What Peter's words mean turns on a single particle, and the witnesses divide over it. Wesley reads the opening clause as meaning since it is thou, holding that the word often bears that sense in ours and in all languages, and concludes that Peter was in no doubt at all, or he would never have quitted the ship. Calvin takes the same clause as a condition and finds the doubt exactly there: Peter had heard Christ speak, so why does he still argue with himself under perplexity? While his faith is small and weak a wish not well considered bursts into a flame; he ought rather to have judged of himself according to his capacity and asked Christ for an increase of faith, whereas now, without the wings of faith, he desires to fly at will, and though the voice of Christ has not its due weight in his heart he wants the waters firm under his feet. Barnes reads the character rather than the grammar and reaches Calvin's verdict: here is the characteristic ardour and rashness of Peter, who had less real faith than he supposed and more ardour than his faith would justify, really attached to Jesus but easily daunted and prone to fall, and was suffered by this to learn his own character and his dependence, a lesson all Christians learn by dear-bought experience. Robertson notes only that the impulsiveness appears as usual, and that Matthew alone preserves the episode.

Whether the request was the right one is where the sharpest difference lies. Clarke condemns it outright, holding that a weak faith is always wishing for signs and miracles, whereas to take Christ at his word argues not only the perfection of faith but the highest exercise of sound reason, since he is to be credited on his own word because he is the Truth and can neither lie nor deceive. Calvin is more careful, allowing that the longing sprang from a good principle but cannot be applauded because it degenerates into a faulty excess, and drawing the rule he wants: wherever the Lord calls we ought to run with alacrity, but whoever proceeds farther will learn from the mournful result what it is to overleap the bounds prescribed to him. Augustine hears in the words the one thing that keeps them from presumption, a confession of what Peter was in himself and of what he expected to receive, so that what no human infirmity was equal to he believed he would be enabled to do.

The single word of permission is read as an act of kindness rather than of indulgence. Gill gives it two purposes, to assure them who he was, since a refusal might have persuaded them it was not Jesus at all, and to commend Peter's love and confirm his faith by a further instance of the power that had brought him there. Clarke draws the general rule and then guards it: however impossible the thing commanded may appear, Christ will certainly give power to accomplish it to those who receive his word by faith, but we must take care never to put that power to the proof for the gratification of a vain curiosity, or even for the strengthening of our own faith while the ordinary means of strengthening it are within reach.
30:
What went wrong is diagnosed the same way by everyone, and the diagnosis is not the weather. Gill describes the wind blowing hard against him and raising waves that beat on him with great violence, but Clarke states the principle: it was by faith in the power of Christ that he was upheld, and when that faith failed, by which the laws of gravitation had been suspended, no wonder those laws returned to their wonted action; it was not the violence of the winds nor the raging of the waves which endangered his life, but his littleness of faith. Ellicott says the same in his own terms, that in the conflict between sight and faith the faith was worsted, and with that came fear, the supernatural strength left him, and the swimmer's art would no longer serve. Wesley presses the last point, that Peter had been used to the sea and was a skilful swimmer, and takes it for a general rule that when grace begins to act the natural courage and strength are withdrawn. Robertson reaches for a phrase about seeing the wind, notes that a fisherman and good swimmer was nevertheless beginning to plunge down, and observes that the cry for rescue stands in a tense that means do it quickly; he adds the remark that it is one thing to see a storm from the deck of a stout ship and another to see it in the midst of the waves. Cyril puts the whole episode the other way round, as a demonstration of what faith can do: Peter was a man like ourselves, made up of flesh and blood and living upon like food, yet while he believed he found his footing safer upon the water than on any ground, and as his faith gradually relaxed his body was drawn down along with it.

The rescue is immediate, and the immediacy is noticed. Gill points to a version that renders it in that very moment, since the case required instant help and Christ was just beside him. Robertson observes that Jesus had to take hold of him and pull him up while still walking on the water himself, and explains the word for doubting from the root meaning twice, a man pulled two ways. Clarke draws the standing lesson: every moment we stand in need of Christ, upheld while we stand by his power only and saved when we have fallen by his mercy alone, so that we should always take care to consider not so much the danger we are exposed to as the power by which we are to be upheld.

The reproof that comes with the hand is read carefully, because it looks harsher than the rescue. Ellicott hears it as loving reproof from one unwilling even here to quench the smoking flax. Calvin insists that in kindly preserving Peter the Lord does not connive at his fault, and then meets the question the words raise, whether every kind of fear proves a weakness of faith. His answer is that Christ reproves the particular doubt which was directly opposed to faith: a man may sometimes doubt without any fault of his own, when the word of the Lord does not speak with certainty on the matter, but Peter had received an express command and had already experienced the power, and abandoned both supports to fall into a foolish fear. Raban turns the outstretched hand into the doctrine it illustrates, that the disciple found a salvation which is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy.
32:
The lull is treated as a further miracle rather than a happy ending. Barnes calls it a new proof of power, since he who has power over winds and waves has all power, and adds from the fourth Gospel that the ship was immediately at the land they were bound for, another wonder in the same collection. Robertson notes that the verb means the wind grew weary and exhausted itself in the presence of its Master, and refuses to call the timing coincidence. Ellicott makes the suddenness the point: for the most part these mountain squalls died away by degrees and left the waves rough, whereas here the wind ceased in a moment, and ceased as the Lord stepped aboard, which is why the other evangelist reports the disciples as astonished above measure. Gill adds a small correction, that Peter came into the ship too but the effect is to be ascribed to Christ's coming and not to his. Clarke reduces it to an aphorism, that Jesus is the Prince of peace and all is peace and calm where he condescends to enter and abide, and Raban had said the same of the heart in which the Lord is present by grace, that there all wars cease.

Ellicott passes on the explanation the other Gospel gives for the astonishment, and it is a hard one: they reflected not on the loaves, for their heart was hardened. He reads this as the disciples' own later analysis of what they had felt that night, and draws the inference that had they taken in the divine creative energy which the feeding involved, nothing afterwards would have seemed startling to them, neither the walking on the waves nor the stilling of the storm.

Who actually made the confession is a real dispute. Clarke thinks the words were probably spoken by the sailors or the passengers and not by the disciples at all, on two grounds: the phrase stands here without the articles that mark the Messianic title, and it would be a strange thing indeed if the disciples, after all the miracles they had seen and after leaving everything to follow him, were only now persuaded that he was the promised one. Ellicott argues from the wording, that the peculiar description of them as those in the ship was meant to distinguish them from Peter and the rest, and probably indicates the crew or some chance passengers with no previous knowledge of him, who in that moment anticipated the faith even of the foremost disciples. Calvin and Gill take the middle position, that the words belong to the disciples and the sailors and other passengers together. Origen alone insists on the opposite, that the disciples in the boat say this and he does not think anyone other than the disciples said it; and he weighs the form of words, which is not the bare confession the two demoniacs had made but one strengthened by an opening asseveration. Robertson leaves the grammar open, allowing that the absence of the article would permit a son of God, as on the centurion's lips at the cross, while holding that they probably meant the full title, and he marks their progress, from the question they had asked about him in the earlier storm toward the confession that is still to come.
34:
Where they landed is described with more care than the name usually gets. Barnes and Clarke both place Gennesaret in Galilee on the western side of the lake, containing Capernaum, where the disciples had been told to steer. Ellicott suggests the name may be a corruption of the older Chinneroth, notes that it gave the lake one of its titles, and calls the region one of singular fertility and among the most populous districts of Palestine; Robertson measures the plain at four miles by two. Henry renders the name as the valley of branches. Calvin declines to settle whether the country was named from the lake or the lake from the country, calling it a matter of little consequence, and Origen and Jerome both say frankly that if they knew what the word meant they could make more of the passage than they can. Raban supplies an etymology anyway, from a power of so modulating its waters as to raise a breeze of its own.

What the people of the district did is treated as the real subject. Henry sets them against their neighbours across the lake, who had besought Christ to depart because they had no occasion for him, while these besought him to help them because they had need of him; and he adds the principle, that Christ reckons it the greatest honour we can do him to make use of him. He also guesses that the report of the crossing helped prepare his welcome in those parts, and thinks that may have been one of the things Christ intended by it, since he has great reaches in what he does. Jerome measures their faith by its range, that they were not content with healing the men of their own country but sent to all the towns round about. Clarke says they knew him again, having already seen his miracles, and collected every diseased person they could find so as to be the instruments of relieving their friends and neighbours.

The request to touch the hem is where several witnesses locate the change. Chrysostom marks the advance: they no longer drag him to their houses or seek the touch of his hand, but draw him by a greater faith, having been taught by the woman with the issue of blood that the hem alone was enough; and he presses the comparison on his hearers, that if those who touched the hem drew such virtue from it, much more shall they who receive his body whole. Ellicott says the same more soberly, that the widespread belief was the natural result of the earlier healing and that the touch implied the faith which was the condition of receiving anything. Gill finds two motives in the request, a confidence that did not doubt of a cure and a sense of unworthiness to be noticed in any nearer way. Robertson allows the element of superstition in it and observes that Jesus honoured the faith regardless.

What the whole summary is for is answered differently by the last two. Calvin reads the evangelists' purpose in the massing of cures: the glory of Christ was attested not by one miracle or another but by a whole region filled with innumerable proofs, the report of which could easily travel to Jerusalem, which is why the ingratitude of a nation that shut its eyes against that brightness was so singularly base; and the reason Christ came was to offer himself as a physician, shadowing out in the healing of bodies something greater. Clarke turns it into a prayer instead, asking what influence the grace and Spirit of Christ must have in the soul when even the border of his garment produced such wonders in bodies, and ending on the petition that our faith be increased so that we may see greater manifestations of his power.
